input.rationale: This turn settles the AddVoter staging question from source, with the library's own tests as the third witness. The public doc comment for AddVoter (api.go:938-941) tells a caller the server is added as a staging server and promoted by the leader once it is ready; membership.md lists catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal and treats staging as a non-voting mode. The implementation does not do that on this path: nextConfiguration's AddVoter case writes Suffrage Voter into the configuration entry that adds the member (configuration.go:234-255), the Staging mode is left only by the Promote case (configuration.go:291-297), and configuration.go's own command table says outright that AddStaging was in fact AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour (configuration.go:101-107). The in-tree unit expectations then show which side is the library's intent: the AddVoter cases expect a Voter for a member that was missing, Staging or Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:185-193), and those expectations mirror the AddStaging cases line for line. So the implementation matches its tested intent and the docs are what mislead: a caller cannot obtain the documented staging phase or the promotion duty through the public API, and the safety-adjacent premise operators plan around - that a fresh member does not count in votes or in the leader's commitment quorum until it has caught up - does not hold for a member added this way. I record that as a scoped documentation-contract defect, keep the counterweights that argue for reading the prose as stale rather than violated, and queue one end-to-end witness that takes one original voter away after the join: if the added member votes, a majority is still reachable and a new command commits; if it were the non-voting member the documentation describes, no majority would remain.

investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.

An end-to-end witness is queued to confirm the consequence that the added member votes immediately.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was that the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist if the only public path that adds a member writes Voter and nothing issues Promote, and reading settles it. The public path is api.go's AddVoter (api.go:946-957), which builds an AddVoter change request; the leader turns that into a configuration entry through nextConfiguration, whose AddVoter case constructs the new server with Suffrage Voter and either replaces the existing entry or appends it (configuration.go:234-255), so the member becomes a voting member in the same entry that introduces it. Staging is a distinct suffrage that only the Promote case leaves (configuration.go:291-297), and no non-test code issues Promote, so the state the documentation describes is unreachable from the public API and the 'promote once ready' duty it promises is owed by nobody. The library itself resolves the contradiction about which side is intended: its command table says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it (configuration.go:101-107), and the unit expectations assert the implemented behavior for AddVoter - a Voter when the member was missing, Staging or Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:185-193) - mirroring the AddStaging cases exactly. The documentation therefore describes a contract the code never had, and a consumer that plans around it is wrong about a safety-adjacent property: contrary to the documented staging phase and the membership note that new servers are caught up before being granted a vote, a member added this way counts in elections and in the leader's quorum from the moment the entry exists. What this claim does not say is that the code is wrong: consensus safety is not broken by it, because the log-comparison rule still keeps a less up-to-date candidate from winning, and the implementation matches its own tests. The defect is the promise in the public documentation, and its practical weight is availability planning rather than safety - quorum arithmetic changes at once, and a member far behind the leader is counted in the commitment quorum while the documented design would not have counted it.
counterevidence: The doc comment is prose, not a test-enforced guarantee, and membership.md is a historical design proposal rather than a contract; a reviewer may reasonably read this as stale documentation to be fixed rather than as a violated requirement.
The unit expectations assert the implemented behavior, so the implementation is deliberate; nothing in the snapshot suggests a partial rollout or a disabled staging path.
Consensus safety is unaffected: a member that has not caught up cannot win an election because voters compare logs, so the mismatch costs availability reasoning rather than correctness.

The documentation does promise a protection, so the account would be defeated if some other public path produced a non-voting member first and promoted it later; no such path was found in the non-test code.
limitations: No execution for this question yet: the account rests on the code, the command table, the doc comment and the unit expectations, and the concrete end-to-end consequence is what the queued witness examines.
This is a documentation-contract finding: it is decidable by reading, and its severity depends on how the maintainers rank the doc comment against the implemented, tested behavior.

scope.description: End-to-end witness on one real cluster: join a fresh, empty node through the public AddVoter API, record the suffrage the leader wrote for that member and the suffrage the new node itself sees, then take one original voter away and record whether a new command still commits - which it can only if the freshly added member counts as a voter.
assumptions: MakeCluster(2) plus MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) merged and fully connected is the in-tree way to join a fresh node (raft_test.go:258-279), and the join itself is the public AddVoter call made by the elected leader.

Disconnecting one original voter is the discriminator: with three voters and one disconnected, a majority needs exactly the remaining original voter plus the new member, so a commit is only reachable if the new member votes; if the new member were the non-voting member the documentation describes, no majority would be reachable.
The apply future is waited on under a bounded interval because the completion of an accepted apply is not bounded by the caller's timeout.

experiment.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real two-node cluster with MakeCluster(2, t, nil) and keeps a copy of the original members, creates a fresh single-node cluster with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1, t, nil), merges the two clusters and fully connects them, then takes the elected leader with c.Leader() and the fresh node as the join target, identifying the other original voter as the peer to remove later. The test then records the suffrage of the new member in the leader's latest configuration and in the new node's own latest configuration, and counts the voters in that configuration. It calls c.Disconnect on the other original voter's address and then applies one command through the public API, waiting on the apply future under a bounded interval and recording apply_with_one_original_voter_gone as committed, an error, or no_completion. Finally it records the new node's last index, the leader's state, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts (the suffrage written for the added member, and whether a command can still commit with one original voter gone) come from the same cluster in one execution.

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. That logFuture has no ShutdownCh, Shutdown() closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown without draining applyCh, and both the main loop and runFSM leave on shutdownCh, so a future left in the buffer has no producer that can respond it: Error() blocks indefinitely and the caller's timeout, which only guarded the enqueue, cannot save it. runLeader's defer responds only futures on leaderState.inflight, so it does not cover a future that was never dispatched. Confirmed by observation: accepted in state Leader, still queued and unresponded after state Shutdown.
investigations.discriminator: Occupy the main loop inside a handler (a public Restore with a caller-supplied reader that stalls on its first Read, which is the handshake), accept one Barrier future through the ordinary public path so it lands in the buffered applyCh, then call Shutdown() and observe whether the future is ever responded: a completion would defeat the suspicion and must name the responding producer, while non-completion together with the future still being queued in applyCh shows the duty was accepted and then lost. Executed: no completion; the duty stayed queued with the node in state Shutdown.

investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. Observed twice, on separate clusters with the same harness: target_ever_leader=false, transfer_err empty, term 2 to 4, original leader back in Leader state, and in both runs the target's term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while the recovery election at term 4 ran one.
investigations.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. interpretations.rationale: Source reading fixes the mechanism without needing a measurement: GetConfiguration() responds a configurationsFuture built from configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} (api.go:900) and getLatestConfiguration only loads the Configuration, not its index (raft.go:2232-2240); Index() is then latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270), i.e. 0. The real index is available in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so this is not a case where the information does not exist, but one where the public producer drops it. The consumer duty is concrete and documented: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry', future.go:27-33), and the documented use of that index is the configuration compare-and-swap: AddVoter and friends describe prevIndex as 'the index of the only configuration upon which this change may be applied; if another configuration entry has been added in the meantime, this request will fail' (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as 'no precondition' (configuration.go:229), so the guard is silently disabled - the request loses the very protection the API promises, and the loss is invisible because the call still succeeds. The same zero is republished as latest_configuration_index in Stats() (api.go:1188), where a constant '0' also misrepresents the node's configuration state to operators. The pending harness (assurance_generated_test.go) is the discriminating observation: it samples the public values next to the main-thread latestIndex on one running bootstrapped leader, which will either confirm the constant zero or defeat the account. Implications are scoped to callers that rely on the index (CAS preconditions, correlating a configuration with a log position); the configuration contents themselves are live and correct, so this is not a consensus-safety defect.
limitations: No execution yet in this turn: the account rests on source reasoning and on the documented API meaning; the harness has been written but has not run, so the observed value is still unknown.
Severity is bounded: callers that ignore Index() are unaffected, and the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

interpretations.rationale: This run was queued to test the one gap I had left explicit, that the earlier vote-less result might have been a timing accident rather than the mechanism. The demotion that makes the target vote-less is performed by the caller in the same run, so the run does not separate the configuration change from the transfer in time.

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.

result.summary: This turn settled the open AddVoter question from source, using the library's own tests as a third witness. The public doc comment says a server added by AddVoter becomes a staging member that the leader promotes once it is ready, and the membership notes list catch-up before granting a vote as a goal; but nextConfiguration writes Suffrage Voter into the very entry that adds the member, Staging is only left by the Promote case, no non-test caller issues Promote, and configuration.go's own command table says AddStaging was in fact AddVoter and deprecates it in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations resolve which side is intended: the AddVoter cases expect a Voter for a member that was missing, Staging or Nonvoter, mirroring the AddStaging cases exactly, so the implementation matches its tested intent and the public documentation is what misleads. I recorded this as one source-decided interpretation with the conclusion explained (source-only answers cannot claim a measured result) and a defect claim scoped to the documented contract, and I kept the counterweights that argue for reading the prose as stale rather than violated, including that consensus safety is unaffected because log comparison still stops a less up-to-date candidate from winning, so the cost is availability planning rather than correctness. The knowledge entry for the immediate-voter behaviour is cited as the relied-on premise by its exact ID and revision. I also queued an end-to-end witness that joins a fresh empty node through the public API, records the suffrage the leader wrote and the suffrage the new node sees, then disconnects one original voter and checks whether a new command still commits - which it can only do if the freshly added member counts as a voter rather than the non-voting member the documentation describes. All three earlier witnessed findings, the configuration index, duties lost at shutdown, and the vote-less transfer with its control and reproduction, remain recorded and are unaffected.

investigations.question: When authority over a node is lost by Shutdown() rather than by stepping down, does an already-accepted Apply/Barrier duty (a logFuture sitting in the buffered applyCh) still have a completion path?
investigations.hypothesis: Apply and Barrier hand the caller a logFuture as soon as the send into applyCh succeeds; with BatchApplyCh the channel is buffered, so acceptance and consumption are separate events. investigations.question: When a caller names a server that holds no vote as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, does the named server acquire leadership, and what happens to the sitting leader's authority?
investigations.hypothesis: LeadershipTransferToServer forwards the caller's id and address to the transfer routine, which only requires a replication state for that server, so a vote-less member is accepted as a target. On that target the TimeoutNow handler sets Candidate and the leadership-transfer flag unconditionally and the candidate loop skips pre-vote because of that flag, so the target runs a real election at term+1; but electSelf casts a self-vote only when the local server is a Voter in the latest configuration, and voters receiving a RequestVote from a member that holds no vote reject it - after already adopting the higher term. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. The requested transfer is therefore unachievable: the named target can never win, while its higher-term vote request deposes the sitting leader, and the caller's future is answered without error because losing leadership during a transfer is reported as success. pickServer shows the implicit path deliberately skips non-voters, so the explicit path accepts an input the implicit path excludes.
history.discriminator: Demote one real follower to a non-voter through the public API, then call LeadershipTransferToServer on that member and sample the real nodes for a bounded interval: whether the named target ever reaches Leader, which servers do lead, whether the original leader still leads at the end, the reported transfer error, and the term before and after. The named target reaching Leader, or leadership staying put with no term movement, would defeat the suspicion.

investigations.question: Does the documented staging phase of AddVoter exist in the implementation: can a server added through the public AddVoter API be a Nonvoter or Staging member that the leader later promotes once it has caught up?
investigations.hypothesis: The public documentation for AddVoter states that the server is added as a staging server and that the leader promotes it to a voter once it is ready, and the membership design notes list catching new servers up before granting them a vote as a main goal. The implementation does not have that phase: nextConfiguration builds the AddVoter entry with Suffrage Voter outright, the separate Staging suffrage is only reachable by an explicit Promote command, and the library's own command documentation says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in its favour. The in-tree unit expectations agree with the implementation, expecting a Voter for a member added through AddVoter from missing, Staging or Nonvoter states, so the state the documentation describes is never entered through the public API and the promotion duty it describes is owed by nobody.
investigations.discriminator: Trace every producer of a configuration entry for AddVoter and every consumer of the Staging suffrage: if the only public path that can add a member writes Suffrage Voter and nothing in the non-test code ever issues Promote, the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist, and the mismatch is decidable by reading rather than by execution. Executed by reading: the AddVoter case writes Voter, Promote is only reached by an explicit Promote command that no non-test caller issues, and the unit expectations for AddVoter match the AddStaging cases. An end-to-end witness is queued to confirm the consequence that the added member votes immediately.

knowledge.assertion: nextConfiguration's AddVoter case writes Suffrage Voter into the very entry that adds the member, so no Staging state is entered on that path and the promotion duty the doc describes is owed by nobody

scope.description: Read, from one running bootstrapped three-node cluster, the public configuration index (GetConfiguration().Index(), Stats()["latest_configuration_index"]) and the main-thread latestIndex/committedIndex of the same node, and emit them as one CA_EVENT JSON line.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) performs a real bootstrap, so the cluster has a real configuration entry at index 1 and a genuinely elected leader.
The configurationsCh request is the same producer path snapshot.go uses to obtain the committed configuration index, so it reads the main thread's authoritative values rather than a supplied premise.
The one committed Apply is only there to move applied/commit indexes past the configuration entry so that the sampled state is unambiguous.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is a single TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. Initialization is the package's own test facility: MakeCluster(3, t, nil) with no injected Config, which bootstraps and elects a leader from real instances in one process; c.Leader() fails the test unless exactly one node is in Leader state. The test then commits one client command through the public Apply API so applied_index and commit_index are past the bootstrapped configuration entry, sends a real configurationsFuture to the leader's configurationsCh (setting ShutdownCh so the request cannot hang) to read the main thread's latestIndex/committedIndex and server count, calls the public GetConfiguration() and Stats() on that same instance, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line containing the leader address, both indexes from the main thread, the public index, both server counts, and the Stats strings, so the comparison is between independently produced values on one node.

scope.description: On one real bootstrapped cluster, accept a Barrier future while the main loop is occupied by a public Restore whose caller-supplied reader stalls, then call Shutdown() and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording whether the accepted future ever completed, how many duties remained queued in applyCh, the channel capacity, and the node state before acceptance and after shutdown.
assumptions: MakeCluster(3, conf) with conf.BatchApplyCh = true is a supported public configuration; BatchApplyCh buffers applyCh to MaxAppendEntries (config.go:169-174), which is what allows acceptance without a consumer.

Occupying the main loop with Restore and a reader that blocks on its first Read models a caller-supplied backup stream that stalls; the reader's first Read is the handshake proving the loop is inside that handler and can no longer select on applyCh.
The control Barrier on the undisturbed leader establishes that the same call does complete while a producer is available, so a later non-completion is not the call being unusable in this harness.
The reader is released after sampling so the occupied handler can return and the node can shut down cleanly; the release happens after the observation and cannot affect it.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It builds a real three-node cluster with MakeCluster(3, t, inmemConfig(t)) after setting BatchApplyCh = true and takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(). First it runs the control: leader.Barrier(0).Error() on the undisturbed leader, recorded as control_barrier_err. Then it occupies the main loop through the public API by calling leader.Restore(&SnapshotMeta{Version:1, Index:1, Term:1, Size:1}, reader, 0) in a goroutine, where reader is a caller-supplied io.Reader whose first Read closes a started channel and then blocks until released; receiving on started is the freeze handshake. While the loop is inside that handler the test accepts the duty through the ordinary public path by calling leader.Barrier(0) in a goroutine and taking the returned future, recording the node state at acceptance. It then calls leader.Shutdown() without waiting on the shutdown future and, for a bounded interval, watches whether duty.Error() ever returns, recording result as no_completion or completed:<err> plus waited_ms; it samples len(leader.applyCh) and cap(leader.applyCh) and the node state afterwards, which shows whether the accepted duty is still sitting in the buffer with no consumer. Finally it releases the reader, records the error the Restore call returns once the handler resumes, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts are the completion result, the queue depth, and the two node states observed on one instance in one execution.

scope.description: On one real four-node cluster, demote one follower to a non-voter through the public API, name it as the target of an explicit leadership transfer, and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the reported transfer error, whether the named target ever reached Leader, which servers led during a bounded interval, the state of the original leader and of the target at the end, and the cluster term before and after.
assumptions: MakeCluster(4, t, nil) gives four real voters and a real leader; DemoteVoter is supported at protocol version 3, so the target stays a connected, log-receiving member of the committed configuration that simply holds no vote.
The target is chosen among nodes actually in Follower state, so it is a viable replication peer and the transfer routine's catch-up wait can be satisfied and the TimeoutNow actually delivered.
The bounded 3 s sampling window only observes leadership outcomes; the claim that a vote-less member cannot win rests on the election code (self-vote and voter gate), not on the window length.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real four-voter cluster with MakeCluster(4, t, nil), takes the single elected leader via c.Leader(), waits for a follower using c.WaitEvent and c.GetInState, and demotes that follower with leader.DemoteVoter(target.localID, 0, 5s), recording demote_err and confirming the target's suffrage from the leader's latest configuration. It samples the maximum current term across c.rafts, then calls leader.LeadershipTransferToServer(target.localID, target.localAddr) through the public API and records the error its future reports. It then polls every 20 ms for up to 3 s across all nodes in c.rafts, recording every address observed in Leader state, whether the named target was ever among them, and whether the original leader led again, and finally records the maximum term after the window and the end states of the original leader and the target. All operands are printed in one CA_EVENT JSON line, so the decisive facts (reported transfer outcome, who led, whether the named target ever led, term movement) come from the same nodes in one execution.

scope.description: Control case on the same explicit leadership-transfer path: on a real four-node cluster, name a server that still holds its vote as the transfer target and emit one CA_EVENT JSON line recording the reported transfer error, whether the named target ever reached Leader, which servers led during a bounded interval, the end states of the original leader and the target, and the term before and after.
assumptions: MakeCluster(4, t, nil) with no demotion is the same cluster shape as the vote-less case, so the configuration, the catch-up wait and the TimeoutNow delivery are unchanged and only the target's suffrage differs.
The target is again chosen from nodes in Follower state, so it is a viable replication peer and the transfer routine's catch-up wait can be satisfied.

The control is a same-cause case, not a requirement check: it separates 'transfer works in this harness' from 'a vote-less target cannot take leadership', and its outcome does not by itself settle the attribution of the earlier term movement.

scope.description: End-to-end witness on one real cluster: join a fresh, empty node through the public AddVoter API, record the suffrage the leader wrote for that member and the suffrage the new node itself sees, then take one original voter away and record whether a new command still commits - which it can only if the freshly added member counts as a voter.
assumptions: MakeCluster(2) plus MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1) merged and fully connected is the in-tree way to join a fresh node (raft_test.go:258-279), and the join itself is the public AddVoter call made by the elected leader.

Disconnecting one original voter is the discriminator: with three voters and one disconnected, a majority needs exactly the remaining original voter plus the new member, so a commit is only reachable if the new member votes; if the new member were the non-voting member the documentation describes, no majority would be reachable.
The apply future is waited on under a bounded interval because the completion of an accepted apply is not bounded by the caller's timeout.

basis.prefix: The harness (draft/assurance_generated_test.go) is one TestAssurance-prefixed test in the captured package. It bootstraps a real two-node cluster with MakeCluster(2, t, nil) and keeps a copy of the original members, creates a fresh single-node cluster with MakeClusterNoBootstrap(1, t, nil), merges the two clusters and fully connects them, then takes the elected leader with c.Leader() and the fresh node as the join target, identifying the other original voter as the peer to remove later. The join is the public leader.AddVoter(newNode.localID, newNode.localAddr, 0, 5s); its future is waited on under a bounded interval, recording add_err and, when it returned, the entry index it reports. The test then records the suffrage of the new member in the leader's latest configuration and in the new node's own latest configuration, and counts the voters in that configuration. It calls c.Disconnect on the other original voter's address and then applies one command through the public API, waiting on the apply future under a bounded interval and recording apply_with_one_original_voter_gone as committed, an error, or no_completion. Finally it records the new node's last index, the leader's state, and prints one CA_EVENT JSON line with all of these operands, so the decisive facts (the suffrage written for the added member, and whether a command can still commit with one original voter gone) come from the same cluster in one execution.

interpretations.rationale: Source reading fixes the mechanism without needing a measurement: GetConfiguration() responds a configurationsFuture built from configurations{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} (api.go:900) and getLatestConfiguration only loads the Configuration, not its index (raft.go:2232-2240); Index() is then latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270), i.e. 0. The real index is available in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so this is not a case where the information does not exist, but one where the public producer drops it. The consumer duty is concrete and documented: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry', future.go:27-33), and the documented use of that index is the configuration compare-and-swap: AddVoter and friends describe prevIndex as 'the index of the only configuration upon which this change may be applied; if another configuration entry has been added in the meantime, this request will fail' (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as 'no precondition' (configuration.go:229), so the guard is silently disabled - the request loses the very protection the API promises, and the loss is invisible because the call still succeeds. The same zero is republished as latest_configuration_index in Stats() (api.go:1188), where a constant '0' also misrepresents the node's configuration state to operators. The pending harness (assurance_generated_test.go) is the discriminating observation: it samples the public values next to the main-thread latestIndex on one running bootstrapped leader, which will either confirm the constant zero or defeat the account. Implications are scoped to callers that rely on the index (CAS preconditions, correlating a configuration with a log position); the configuration contents themselves are live and correct, so this is not a consensus-safety defect.
limitations: No execution yet in this turn: the account rests on source reasoning and on the documented API meaning; the harness has been written but has not run, so the observed value is still unknown.
Severity is bounded: callers that ignore Index() are unaffected, and the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was: if the public values track the real index the hypothesis is wrong, if the public values stay 0 while the main-thread index is >= 1 it holds. The completed execution reports exactly the second case on one node and one sample: main_latest_index=1 and main_committed_index=1 (3 voter servers) read from the main thread, public_index=0 with public_servers=3 read from GetConfiguration(), and stats_latest_configuration_index="0" beside the same three-voter latest_configuration, with commit_index=3 and applied_index=3 showing the node was well past the configuration entry. Both values came from the same runtime object inside one execution, so this is a within-node comparison rather than a cross-scenario join. The account of why is source-fixed and independent of the sample: GetConfiguration() constructs configurationsFuture{latest: r.getLatestConfiguration()} and responds it immediately (api.go:900), getLatestConfiguration loads only the Configuration from the atomic copy (raft.go:2232-2240), and Index() is the never-assigned latestIndex of that struct (future.go:267-270); no code path assigns it for this future, so the constant is a property of the constructor rather than an artefact of one sample. The real index does exist in-process - the main loop answers configurationsCh with r.configurations.Clone(), which carries latestIndex and committedIndex (raft.go:889) and is what snapshot.go consumes - so the public producer drops a value the target itself publishes elsewhere. The consumer duty is what makes this consequential rather than cosmetic: ConfigurationFuture embeds IndexFuture ('Index holds the index of the newly applied log entry'), and the documented use of that index is the configuration precondition - AddVoter and its siblings describe prevIndex as the index of the only configuration upon which the change may be applied, failing if another configuration entry intervened (api.go:941-944). A caller that reads the index from the only public source and passes it back supplies 0, and nextConfiguration treats prevIndex == 0 as no precondition (configuration.go:229), so the request keeps the same return value while silently losing the protection it was composed around; the same 0 is republished as latest_configuration_index (api.go:1188), where a constant also misdescribes the node's configuration state to an operator. Scope is bounded and stated: the configuration contents are live and correct and no consensus decision is taken on this value, so this is a basis/contract defect for index-dependent callers, not a safety violation.

answers.031156ce4e3d4bf5a8845619024ff0c4-gap-0: Observed on the elected leader of a bootstrapped three-node cluster (CheckRun dd34591ecee5442ca8f7b8c478709f1b, parsed event 0): GetConfiguration().Index() carried 0 while the main thread's latest and committed configuration index for the same node was 1 with 3 voter servers, and Stats()["latest_configuration_index"] carried the same "0" beside a non-empty latest_configuration; the public value does not track the real index.

knowledge.assertion: GetConfiguration() carries only the Configuration (latestIndex left zero), so ConfigurationFuture.Index() is 0 on every call while the main thread holds the real latest configuration index
nextConfiguration enforces prevIndex only when it is > 0, so the 0 returned by the public API disables the documented configuration compare-and-swap

counterevidence: The captured tree is byte-identical to the released upstream copy of the same revision, and no assertion or test in the snapshot requires ConfigurationFuture.Index() to be non-zero, so the judgment that the zero is a defect rather than an intended 'there is no index to report here' reading rests on the documented meaning of Index() and of prevIndex rather than on a violated in-tree expectation.

The witness is one node in one execution; the claim that the value is constant rests on the constructor and on the absence of any writer to that field for this future (api.go:895-903, future.go:255-270), not on repeated sampling.
limitations: Only the index value is shown to be wrong; the returned Configuration is the true latest configuration, and callers that ignore Index() are unaffected.
The impact chain to the disabled precondition is source-based: the execution exercised the read path, not a configuration change issued with the returned 0 as prevIndex.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved in the direction that supports the defect account, and the decisive operands come from one instance in one execution rather than from a join across scenarios: control_barrier_err is empty (the same Barrier call completed on the undisturbed leader, so acceptance and completion work when a producer exists), freeze_handshake is inside_restore_read (the main loop was inside its own restore handler and could not select on applyCh again), state_at_accept is Leader and duty_accepted is true (the public API handed the caller a future), state_after_shutdown is Shutdown, and the observation reports result=no_completion over a 3000 ms interval with queued_in_apply_ch=1 and apply_ch_capacity=64 - the accepted duty was still sitting in the buffer, with no consumer, after authority was lost. restore_after_release='failed to write snapshot: unexpected EOF' shows that the occupied handler was the node's main loop and that it did resume once the reader was released, which also rules out the harness having wedged the node in some other way. The interval is stated as what it is: 3000 ms of non-progress is not by itself the evidence for indefinite blocking; the indefinite part is source-fixed, and it is why the future can never be woken - deferError.Error() waits on the internal error channel alone once respond has not been called (future.go:113-118), and this logFuture is created without a ShutdownCh, unlike the internal restore and snapshot futures that do get one (raft.go:1169, raft.go:1914, snapshot.go:152); Shutdown() only closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown (api.go:1012-1025) while both the main loop and runFSM leave on that channel; and runLeader's defer responds only the futures already recorded on leaderState.inflight (raft.go:502-560), which a duty that never left applyCh is not. The duty was therefore accepted, its basis (a live leader to dispatch it) disappeared, and the accepted obligation was neither cancelled with a reason nor transferred: it was dropped silently, which is exactly the failure the repository's own test file flags for this family at raft_test.go:40-42. The condition that makes it reachable is the documented one: BatchApplyCh decouples acceptance from consumption (config.go:169-174), and the same comment concedes it breaks the timeout guarantee on Apply, so a caller that trusts a positive timeout to bound its wait is not protected.

answers.f2c2b4e0415449d4941c8e53ffbc722e-gap-1: No producer responded the accepted Barrier future after Shutdown(), and the duty was still queued at that point: with the leader occupied inside its own Restore handler, the Barrier future was accepted in state Leader and, after Shutdown() moved the node to state Shutdown, the future had not been responded within the 3000 ms observation while len(applyCh)=1 of capacity 64 (CheckRun c5d127c955b549a8888fe6bab568dbce, parsed event 0).

knowledge.assertion: the timeout guards only the enqueue into applyCh and the returned logFuture has no ShutdownCh, so no timeout- or shutdown-bounded completion follows acceptance
Shutdown() leaves applyCh undrained and runLeader's defer responds only leaderState.inflight futures, so the queued duty has no remaining producer

counterevidence: The reachable window needs the main loop to be occupied at the moment of acceptance and shutdown; the harness makes that deterministic with a caller-supplied reader that stalls, so the execution shows the mechanism, not a frequency of occurrence under spontaneous timing.

The window also needs BatchApplyCh (config.go:169-174); with the default unbuffered applyCh the enqueue itself is the handoff, so the same duty would instead be rejected at enqueue via the caller's timeout or shutdownCh escape in Apply.

The node was in the middle of an orderly shutdown, so one can argue a shutting-down node owes nothing in flight; the defect account rests on the narrower observation that the API had already accepted the duty and returned a future whose Error() has no shutdown notice and no timeout, leaving the caller unable to distinguish dropped from pending.
limitations: Single node and single execution; the claim that no completion path remains rests on the source argument above (no writer to the error channel after shutdown; every completer exits on shutdownCh), not on repeated sampling or on an unbounded wait.

Only the Barrier path was executed. VerifyLeader constructs its verifyFuture without a ShutdownCh too and sends it on a 64-buffered channel (api.go:883-893, api.go:568), so it shares the shape, but that is a source-level observation and was not exercised.
The scenario models a slow caller-supplied stream keeping the handler busy; it does not claim that shutdown always finds a duty in the buffer.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator resolved against the harmless reading: the named target never reached Leader, so the transfer did not accomplish what the API call names. The decisive operands from that one execution are target_suffrage=Nonvoter (the target really held no vote, confirmed from the leader's latest configuration), transfer_err empty (the caller was told the transfer was not a failure), target_ever_leader=false with target_state_at_end=Follower, leaders_seen containing only the original leader, and term_before=2 to term_after=4. The impossibility is source-fixed and independent of the window: a server without a vote has no self-vote in electSelf (a vote is cast only when the iterated server's Suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), voters reject its RequestVote after the term adoption that precedes the rejection (raft.go:1664-1684), and a non-voter never starts an election on its own (raft.go:242-250) - so no vote-less member can ever be elected in this revision, and the explicit transfer path accepted one anyway because it only looks for a replication state (raft.go:765-783). The cost side is what the term movement shows: the transfer candidate ran a real election (TimeoutNow sets Candidate and the transfer flag, raft.go:2209-2214, and that flag suppresses pre-vote in the candidate loop, raft.go:294-300), voters adopted the higher term and stepped down before rejecting, and with the term at 4 the sitting leader at term 2 cannot still have been leader, so leadership was lost and had to be re-won. The asymmetry with the implicit path, which deliberately skips non-voters when picking a server (raft.go:2163-2182), shows the explicit input is accepted where the implicit path would have refused it. The report to the caller is the part that turns this from an operator mistake into a defect of the library: the transfer case answers nil when leadership is lost during a transfer because that is the expected outcome (raft.go:734-739), so a caller that named a vote-less server receives the same success signal as a caller whose transfer worked, and cannot tell that authority never reached the named node.

answers.721c1688d0604614841236bb40a995b2-gap-2: No: the named vote-less target never acquired leadership (target_ever_leader=false over the 3 s window, ending in state Follower) while the caller's future reported no error (transfer_err empty), and the cluster's maximum term advanced from 2 to 4 with the original leader in Leader state at the end (CheckRun 2b61659461634c04b53ec61c35541227, parsed event 0). Source shows the negative is structural: a non-voter gets no self-vote and voters reject its request.

counterevidence: This execution contains no same-window control, so the term advance is attributed to the transfer campaign on the source argument that a Leader never campaigns itself and that a voter adopts a higher term before rejecting it; the control just queued (same path, voter target) separates 'the mechanism does not work here' from 'the mechanism works and a vote-less target cannot take the leadership', but it does not by itself exclude spontaneous election noise in a 3 s window.

The end state is the same as the start (the original leader leads again), so a caller that inspects only who leads afterwards sees no damage; the observed harm is the term movement and the inferred loss of leadership in between, not a lasting loss.

The target's vote was removed by the caller's own previous API call in the same run, so this is not a case where the library silently mis-states an operator-managed configuration; the operator asked for the demotion, then asked for a transfer to the demoted node.
limitations: Single execution and a single target; the claim that a vote-less member can never win rests on the election code paths above, not on repeated runs.

The caller's success value is explained by the lost-leadership branch (raft.go:734-739); the same CheckRun's DEBUG log names that branch ('lost leadership during transfer (expected)'), which corroborates the reading but is the library's own message text rather than an independent probe of the returned value.

The intermediate sequence is observed in the run's own log rather than merely inferred: at 16:26:25.836 the target enters candidate state at term=3 with no pre-vote success line and asks all three voters for a vote while never logging a self-vote, each voter logs term adoption ('lost leadership because received a requestVote with a newer term') immediately followed by 'rejecting vote request since node is not a voter: from=927e473c...', and at 16:26:25.894 the original leader campaigns at term=4 (pre-vote tally 2 of votesNeeded 2) and re-enters leader state; these are the library's own log messages, while the sampled CA_EVENT operands remain the states, term endpoints and window.

Because the term-3 campaign skipped pre-vote while both genuine elections in the same run recorded a successful pre-vote first, the log also distinguishes the transfer path from an ordinary election; what it does not provide is a run of the same window without the transfer call, which is why the control case is queued rather than assumed.

interpretations.rationale: The control predicate was that the same call with a voter as the named target does move leadership to that server, and it holds: the target was the only leader observed, ended in Leader state, the original leader ended in Follower and never led again, and the term moved 2 to 3, a single step. That matters twice over for the question about vote-less targets. First, it removes the alternative that the explicit transfer path is simply inoperative in this harness, because the identical call delivered leadership when the target had a vote; combined with the source facts that a non-voter casts no self-vote (a vote is cast only for servers whose suffrage is Voter, raft.go:2015-2040), that voters reject its RequestVote after adopting its higher term (raft.go:1664-1684), and that a non-voter never starts an election by itself (raft.go:242-250), the failure to transfer is attributable to the target's lacking a vote rather than to the harness or to the call. Second, it makes the cost of the vote-less attempt visible relative to the intended path: the successful transfer advanced the term by one and placed the named server in charge, while the vote-less attempt advanced the term by two (the campaign at term 3 and the re-election at term 4 seen in that run's log) and left the same server as a follower, so the request consumed an extra election and returned no benefit. It also corrects my earlier emphasis: transfer_err was empty in both cases, so the empty error is not what marks the failure - in the control it accompanies success. The discriminating evidence is the pair of outcomes (target_ever_leader true with one term step, versus false with two term steps) plus the two source arguments, and the caller-visible gap remains that both callers receive the same success signal while only one of them had authority moved to the named node. The current account is therefore unchanged in substance and better bounded: the defect is that the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership and reports success, and I keep the residual uncertainty about timing variation rather than smoothing it away, which is what the queued repeat of the vote-less case examines.
counterevidence: The two cases are separate executions on separate clusters, not a randomized paired trial, so run-to-run timing variation is not excluded by the pair alone; what the pair excludes is the specific alternative that the transfer mechanism does not work in this harness, and the queued repeat tests whether the vote-less non-transfer and its two-step term cost recur.
An empty transfer error occurs in both cases, so it cannot be used as the distinguishing signal; the earlier account leaned on that value and is narrowed here to the outcome and term-cost operands.

In the control the original leader ended as a follower without leading again, while in the vote-less case leadership stayed with the original server; a caller watching only the final leader could therefore see the vote-less request as harmless, and the harm is the wasted election cycle rather than a lasting loss.
limitations: Each case is a single execution with a single target chosen among followers; neither case repeats a target of the other suffrage type more than once, so the comparison rests on two runs plus the source paths.

The 3 s window bounds what is observed; the claim that a vote-less member can never win is source-based, and the term-movement comparison is an endpoint-to-endpoint difference, not a trace of every intermediate term value.

The vote-less case's target had been demoted by the caller in the same run, so the configuration change and the transfer are not separated in time in that execution; the control has no such change, which is a second difference between the two runs besides suffrage.
interpretations.joint_history: The control and the vote-less case are two executions of the same harness shape on separate fresh clusters of the same shape (MakeCluster(4) with default config, one elected leader, a follower chosen from Follower state as target, 3 s sampling every 20 ms). They differ in exactly one input: in the vote-less case the target is first demoted by a committed DemoteVoter, in the control it keeps its vote. They are independent executions rather than one split history, so the pair supports a same-cause comparison (transition works with a vote, does not deliver without one) and does not by itself exclude run-to-run timing variation.

interpretations.rationale: This run was queued to test the one gap I had left explicit, that the earlier vote-less result might have been a timing accident rather than the mechanism. The reproduction is exact on every operand: target_suffrage=Nonvoter, transfer_err empty, target_ever_leader=false with the target ending as Follower, the original leader the only server seen leading and in Leader state at the end, and the term advancing 2 to 4 - the same two-step cost as the first run, against a single step for the voter-target control. The second run's log repeats the internal sequence as well: the target enters candidate state at term 3 with no pre-vote lines of its own while both genuine elections in that run record pre-voting for self and a pre-vote success, each voter logs adopting the higher term immediately before rejecting a node that is not a voter, and the recovery election at term 4 is a real pre-voted election won by the original server with tally 2 of votesNeeded 2. That is the mechanism the sources predict - a candidate that holds no vote gets no self-vote, cannot be granted one by voters, and yet moves the term it runs at, so the caller spends an election and receives no transfer - and it now holds for two independent executions. What the repeat does not buy is a broader sample: both runs use the same fixed harness, the same cluster size and the same sequence of caller steps, so this is schedule variation on one scenario, and I keep that as the boundary of the claim rather than treating two runs as generality. The defect account for the question is unchanged and now reproducible: the explicit transfer path accepts a target that cannot hold leadership, moves no authority to it, and reports the same success value it reports when a real transfer succeeds (the control also reported an empty error), so the caller cannot distinguish a transfer that happened from one that never could.
counterevidence: Both runs come from the same fixed harness with the same inputs, so the repetition tests scheduling variation of one scenario rather than a range of cluster sizes, timings or target choices; the source argument for the impossibility of a vote-less winner is what covers those unobserved variants.

As in the earlier control, an empty transfer error accompanies both the successful and the unsuccessful case, so the empty value is not evidence of failure by itself and the account rests on the outcome and term-cost operands.
The demotion that makes the target vote-less is performed by the caller in the same run, so the run does not separate the configuration change from the transfer in time.
limitations: Two runs, one scenario: the reproduction is exact but narrow, and the claim that a vote-less member can never win still rests on the election code paths rather than on sampling many configurations.

The term cost is compared as an endpoint-to-endpoint difference between runs; the intermediate steps are corroborated by the library's own log messages, not by an independent probe of the term value at each instant.

interpretations.rationale: The declared discriminator was that the documented staging phase and its promotion duty do not exist if the only public path that adds a member writes Voter and nothing issues Promote, and reading settles it. The public path is api.go's AddVoter (api.go:946-957), which builds an AddVoter change request; the leader turns that into a configuration entry through nextConfiguration, whose AddVoter case constructs the new server with Suffrage Voter and either replaces the existing entry or appends it (configuration.go:234-255), so the member becomes a voting member in the same entry that introduces it. Staging is a distinct suffrage that only the Promote case leaves (configuration.go:291-297), and no non-test code issues Promote, so the state the documentation describes is unreachable from the public API and the 'promote once ready' duty it promises is owed by nobody. The library itself resolves the contradiction about which side is intended: its command table says AddStaging was actually AddVoter and is deprecated in favour of it (configuration.go:101-107), and the unit expectations assert the implemented behavior for AddVoter - a Voter when the member was missing, Staging or Nonvoter (configuration_test.go:185-193) - mirroring the AddStaging cases exactly. The documentation therefore describes a contract the code never had, and a consumer that plans around it is wrong about a safety-adjacent property: contrary to the documented staging phase and the membership note that new servers are caught up before being granted a vote, a member added this way counts in elections and in the leader's quorum from the moment the entry exists. What this claim does not say is that the code is wrong: consensus safety is not broken by it, because the log-comparison rule still keeps a less up-to-date candidate from winning, and the implementation matches its own tests. The defect is the promise in the public documentation, and its practical weight is availability planning rather than safety - quorum arithmetic changes at once, and a member far behind the leader is counted in the commitment quorum while the documented design would not have counted it.
counterevidence: The doc comment is prose, not a test-enforced guarantee, and membership.md is a historical design proposal rather than a contract; a reviewer may reasonably read this as stale documentation to be fixed rather than as a violated requirement.
The unit expectations assert the implemented behavior, so the implementation is deliberate; nothing in the snapshot suggests a partial rollout or a disabled staging path.
Consensus safety is unaffected: a member that has not caught up cannot win an election because voters compare logs, so the mismatch costs availability reasoning rather than correctness.

The documentation does promise a protection, so the account would be defeated if some other public path produced a non-voting member first and promoted it later; no such path was found in the non-test code.
limitations: No execution for this question yet: the account rests on the code, the command table, the doc comment and the unit expectations, and the concrete end-to-end consequence is what the queued witness examines.
This is a documentation-contract finding: it is decidable by reading, and its severity depends on how the maintainers rank the doc comment against the implemented, tested behavior.

These are the main goals:
 - Bringing things in line with the description in my PhD dissertation;
 - Catching up new servers prior to granting them a vote, as well as allowing permanent non-voting members; and
 - Eliminating the `peers.json` file, to avoid issues of consistency between that and the log/snapshot.

- *Nonvoter*: a server that receives log entries but is not considered for elections or commitment purposes.
 - *Staging*: a server that acts like a nonvoter with one exception: once a staging server receives enough log entries to catch up sufficiently to the leader's log, the leader will invoke a  membership change to change the staging server to a voter.

All changes to the configuration will be done by writing a new configuration to the log. The new configuration will be in affect as soon as it is appended to the log (not when it is committed like a normal state machine command). Note that, per my dissertation, there can be at most one uncommitted configuration at a time (the next configuration may not be created until the prior one has been committed). It's not strictly necessary to follow these same rules for the nonvoter/staging servers, but we think its best to treat all changes uniformly.
